title: How Does Your Mouse Know Where You Moved It?
sources: HowStuffWorks 'How Does an Optical Mouse Work?' (computer.howstuffworks.com/question631.htm): a small red LED bounces light off the surface onto a CMOS sensor; a tiny camera takes about 1,500 pictures every second; a DSP detects patterns in the images and how they moved since the previous image

Wikipedia 'Optical mouse': the sensor is essentially a tiny low-resolution video camera capturing a thousand or more images per second; images compared by cross correlation to compute the offset; most optical mice do not work properly on glass or polished, transparent surfaces (cursor drifts)

ETHW 'Milestones: Invention of SRI's Computer Mouse, 1961-1968': first prototype built fall 1964 by Bill English for Douglas Engelbart, a wooden block with two perpendicular metal wheels; nicknamed 'mouse' because the cord emerged from the back like a tail

Computer History Museum, Revolution: Input & Output (computerhistory.org/revolution/input-output/14/350): original wooden Engelbart mouse prototype; Engelbart: 'It just looked like a mouse with a tail, and we all called it that.'

lines.text: How does your mouse know where you moved it?
lines.caps: HOW DOES YOUR *MOUSE | KNOW *WHERE YOU | *MOVED IT?

lines.text: Flip it over, and there's a little red light
lines.caps: FLIP IT *OVER | AND THERE'S A *LITTLE | *RED LIGHT

lines.text: right next to a tiny camera
snapping over a thousand pictures a second.
Even a smooth desk is full of tiny bumps,
lines.caps: EVEN A *SMOOTH DESK | IS *FULL | OF TINY *BUMPS

lines.text: so a chip compares each picture to the last,
sees how far the bumps slid,
and moves your cursor to match.
That's why it goes crazy on glass.
There's nothing for the camera to grab onto.
And the very first mouse, from nineteen sixty four,
was a wooden box on two metal wheels,
nicknamed a mouse because its cord looked like a tail.
lines.caps: *NICKNAMED A MOUSE | BECAUSE ITS *CORD | LOOKED LIKE A *TAIL
